walkthroughs.body_html:
Run for Your Life — a core area of A-Level Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Run for Your Life brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Run for Your Life.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: According to the sliding filament theory, contraction happens because:
options: myosin heads pull actin filaments inwards, shortening the sarcomere
the actin and myosin filaments themselves get shorter
muscle cells split to halve their length
the Z-lines grow longer

mcqs.q: The immediate energy source for muscle contraction is:
options: ATP
glucose
lactate
creatine alone

mcqs.q: Anaerobic respiration in human muscle produces:
options: lactate
ethanol and carbon dioxide
carbon dioxide and water
oxygen

mcqs.q: After sprinting, the oxygen debt is repaid in order to:
options: oxidise the lactate that accumulated
rebuild the broken sarcomeres
cool the muscles directly
replace lost red blood cells

mcqs.q: What actually shortens during muscle contraction?
options: The actin and myosin filaments themselves get shorter.
The actin and myosin filaments slide past each other, shortening the sarcomere; the filaments themselves do not shorten.
The muscle cells split in half to shorten the muscle.
Lactic acid is produced only in the liver, never in muscle.
Lactic acid is produced only in the liver, never in muscle.
Lactic acid is produced because too much oxygen reaches the muscle.
No - lactate is produced in anaerobic respiration when oxygen is short, and is later oxidised when oxygen returns.
ATP is made only in the blood and delivered to muscle.

mcqs.q: Is ATP a long-term energy store for muscles?
options: The muscle cells split in half to shorten the muscle.
No - ATP is the immediate energy currency and is recycled constantly; muscles store energy as glycogen.
Muscles store large amounts of ATP ready for exercise.
ATP is made only in the blood and delivered to muscle.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Oxygen debt”?
options: The extra oxygen taken in after exercise to oxidise the lactate that built up during anaerobic respiration.
Muscle contraction in which myosin heads bind actin and pull the thin filaments past the thick filaments, shortening each sarcomere.
The functional contractile unit of a myofibril, running between two Z-lines and containing overlapping actin and myosin filaments.
The immediate energy currency of cells; its hydrolysis to ADP and inorganic phosphate releases energy that powers muscle contraction.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Sarcomere”?
options: The immediate energy currency of cells; its hydrolysis to ADP and inorganic phosphate releases energy that powers muscle contraction.
The functional contractile unit of a myofibril, running between two Z-lines and containing overlapping actin and myosin filaments.
Muscle contraction in which myosin heads bind actin and pull the thin filaments past the thick filaments, shortening each sarcomere.
Respiration without oxygen that produces lactate in muscle, giving a small but rapid ATP yield and causing an oxygen debt.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Sliding filament theory”?
options: The complete oxidation of glucose using oxygen in the mitochondria, releasing a large yield of ATP plus carbon dioxide and water.
Respiration without oxygen that produces lactate in muscle, giving a small but rapid ATP yield and causing an oxygen debt.
The extra oxygen taken in after exercise to oxidise the lactate that built up during anaerobic respiration.
Muscle contraction in which myosin heads bind actin and pull the thin filaments past the thick filaments, shortening each sarcomere.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Anaerobic respiration”?
options: The extra oxygen taken in after exercise to oxidise the lactate that built up during anaerobic respiration.
Respiration without oxygen that produces lactate in muscle, giving a small but rapid ATP yield and causing an oxygen debt.
The functional contractile unit of a myofibril, running between two Z-lines and containing overlapping actin and myosin filaments.
Muscle contraction in which myosin heads bind actin and pull the thin filaments past the thick filaments, shortening each sarcomere.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “ATP”?
options: The immediate energy currency of cells; its hydrolysis to ADP and inorganic phosphate releases energy that powers muscle contraction.
Muscle contraction in which myosin heads bind actin and pull the thin filaments past the thick filaments, shortening each sarcomere.
Respiration without oxygen that produces lactate in muscle, giving a small but rapid ATP yield and causing an oxygen debt.
The functional contractile unit of a myofibril, running between two Z-lines and containing overlapping actin and myosin filaments.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Aerobic respiration”?
options: The complete oxidation of glucose using oxygen in the mitochondria, releasing a large yield of ATP plus carbon dioxide and water.
The immediate energy currency of cells; its hydrolysis to ADP and inorganic phosphate releases energy that powers muscle contraction.
The functional contractile unit of a myofibril, running between two Z-lines and containing overlapping actin and myosin filaments.
Respiration without oxygen that produces lactate in muscle, giving a small but rapid ATP yield and causing an oxygen debt.

free_texts.hint: It's one of the six key terms above.

sequence.def: Glucose split into 2 pyruvate in cytoplasm; net 2 ATP
Pyruvate -> acetyl-CoA in matrix; CO2 released
Acetyl-CoA oxidised; makes NADH, FADH2 and CO2
NADH/FADH2 donate electrons along inner membrane
ATP synthase makes most ATP; O2 is final acceptor
